metadata.title: Collins v. Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115 (1992) (No. 90-1279)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Collins v. Harker Heights

Opinion filed: 1992-02-26

Docket No.: 90-1279

Citations:
• 117 L. Ed. 2d 261
• 112 S. Ct. 1061
• 503 U.S. 115
• 1992 U.S. LEXIS 1376

Case holding summaries:
• reaffirming "shock[s] the conscience" standard in civil damage actions for violations of substantive due process
• aﬃrming dismissal of due process claims by widow of city worker who was asphyxiated during under- ground utility work, despite allegations of deliberate indiﬀer- ence
• "The employment relationship . . . is not of controlling signifi- cance."
• constitutional violation must be product of official custom or policy to hold municipality liable
• "arbitrary government action that must `shock the conscience' of federal judges"
• expressing reluctance "to expand the concept of substantive due process"
• matters involving competing and multifaceted social and policy decisions best left to local decisionmaking
• "the Due Process Clause of its own force requires that conditions of confinement satisfy certain minimal standards for pretrial detainees"
• expressing “reluctan[ce] to expand the concept of substantive due process because guideposts for responsible decisionmaking in this unchartered area are scarce and open-ended”
• failure to train and warn city employees to avoid dangers present in their work place not a due process deprivation
• “As a general matter, the Court has always been reluctant to expand the concept of substantive due process because guideposts for responsible decisionmaking in this unchartered area are scarce and open-ended.”
• "Due Process Clause of its own force requires that conditions of confinement satisfy certain minimum standards... for persons in mental institutions"
• resolving § 1983 claims against municipalities requires consideration of whether “the city is responsible” for harm “caused by a constitutional violation”
• noting that the Due Process Clause was intended to prevent government officials "` "from abusing [their] power, or employing it as an instrument of oppression"` "
• emphasizing "the separate character of the inquiry into the question of municipal responsibility and the question of whether a constitutional violation occurred,"
• explaining that the Due Process Clause “requires that conditions of confinement satisfy certain minimum standards for pretrial 8 No. 02-1873 detainees, for people in mental institutions, for convicted felons, and for persons under arrest”
• explaining that "deliberate indifference" in training employees provides the necessary causal link to hold a municipality liable for the torts of its employees
• “[A city] is only liable when it can be fairly said that the city itself is the wrongdoer.”
• "Although the statute provides the citizen with an effective remedy against those abuses of state power that violate federal law, it does not provide a remedy for abuses that do not violate federal law[.]"
• intimating that an even more exacting requirement, deliberate or intentional conduct, should be applied
• No remedy under 1983 for employee's death.
• stating that a municipality is only liable when the municipality itself is the "wrongdoer"
• recognizing that municipal liability requires an underlying constitutional violation
• "if a city employee violates another's constitutional rights, the city may be liable if it had a policy or custom of failing to train its employees and that failure to train caused the constitutional violation"
• "proper analysis requires us to separate two different issues when a § 1983 claim is asserted against a municipality: (1) whether plaintiff's harm was caused by a constitutional violation and (2
• "proper analysis requires us to separate two different issues when a § 1983 claim is asserted against a municipality: (1) whether plaintiff's harm was caused by a constitutional violation and (2) if so, whether the city is responsible for that violation"
• "The most familiar office of [the Due Process] Clause is to provide a guarantee of fair procedure in connection with any deprivation of life, liberty or property . . ."
• counseling caution when determining whether "to expand the concept of substantive due process because guideposts for responsible decisionmaking in this unchartered area are scarce and open-ended"
• noting previous rejections of claims purporting to interpret the Due Process Clause to create federal duties that are traditionally created by state tort law
• "proper analysis requires us to separate two different issues when a 1983 claim is asserted against a municipality: (1) whether plaintiff's harm was caused by a constitutional violation, and (2) if so, whether the city is responsible for that violation."
• employment relationship alone cannot give rise to constitutional duty to protect
• "As a general matter, [we have] always been reluctant to expand the concept of substantive due process because guideposts for responsible decisionmaking in this unchartered area are scarce and open-ended."
• holding that the Due Process Clause does not "guarantee municipal employees a workplace that is free of unreasonable risks of harm"
• identifying two issues that must be analyzed in any § 1983 claim"(1) whether plaintiffs harm was caused by a constitutional violation, and (2) if so, whether the city is responsible for that violation"
• “The Court has always been reluctant to expand the concept of substantive due process . . . The doctrine of judicial self-restraint requires [courts] to exercise the utmost care whenever . . . asked to break new ground in this field.”
• applying failure to train theory to city sanitation workers
• Due Process Clause "protects individual liberty against `certain government actions regardless of the fairness of the procedures used to implement them'"
• rejecting claim that the Due Process Clause imposes a duty on government employers to provide its employees with a safe working environment
• recognizing that the Due Process Clause does not "impose federal duties that are analogous to those traditionally imposed by state tort law"
• court must look to the complaint for a description of the constitutional right at stake
• "[P]roper analysis requires us to separate two different issues when a § 1983 claim is asserted against a municipality: (1) whether plaintiff's harm was caused by a constitutional violation, and (2
• "[P]roper analysis requires us to separate two different issues when a § 1983 claim is asserted against a municipality: (1) whether plaintiff's harm was caused by a constitutional violation, and (2) if so, whether the city is responsible for that violation."
• no due process 6 violation where plaintiff alleged the city failed to 7 properly train or warn its employees of known dangers that 8 resulted in sanitation worker’s asphyxiation
• noting that the Due Process Clause was intended to prevent government officials "from abusing [their] power, or employing it as an instrument of oppression"
• "Neither the text nor the history of the Due Process Clause supports petitioner's claim that the government employer's duty to provide its employees with a safe working environment is a substantive component of the Due Process Clause."
• stating that the Court is not persuaded that the defendants’ actions “can properly be characterized as arbitrary, or conscience shocking, in a constitutional sense”
• " 'Historically, this guarantee of due process has been applied to deliberate decisions of government officials to deprive a person of life, liberty, or property.' "
• holding that city’s conduct did not violate the Due Process Clause “[e]ven though [it] may be actionable under state law”
• stating that, to survive summary judgment on substantive due process claim, plaintiff must point to record evidence that defendants “intended to injure or to spite” him by insisting on broad release for disclosure of personal medical information
• describing "deliberate indifference" as used in City of Canton
